title: How to Improve Cold Email Deliverability: A Fix-It Playbook
metaTitle: How to Improve Cold Email Deliverability (2026)
metaDescription: Deliverability took a hit? Work through the fixes in this order: authentication, blacklists, list quality, volume, content, then reputation repair. A diagnostic walkthrough, step by step.
excerpt: When deliverability drops, fixing things in the wrong order costs you days you don't have. This is the diagnostic sequence I actually work through, fastest fix first.

toc.title: First, verify there's a real problem

contentHtml:
The instinct when deliverability slips is to rewrite the email. That's almost never where the real problem lives. There's an actual order to fixing this, running from fastest and most common down to slowest, and working through it out of sequence just burns days you don't need to lose.

Below is the exact sequence I run. Start at step one, and don't move to the next until the current one is genuinely clean.

First, verify there's a real problem

A dropping open rate isn't proof of a deliverability issue on its own. Open tracking is unreliable — plenty of clients block or pre-fetch it. Get an actual measurement before you touch anything.

Run an inbox placement test from the affected mailbox. If mail is landing in primary, your issue is targeting or copy, not deliverability. If it's going to spam or not arriving at all, keep working down this list.

Step 1: Check your authentication

This is the most common culprit and the quickest one to fix, which is why it comes first. Broken or missing SPF, DKIM, or DMARC signals to mailbox providers that you're unverified, and in 2026 that alone is often enough to route you straight to spam.

Run your sending domain through the free SPF, DKIM and DMARC checker. All three need to pass. One common, quiet failure mode: an SPF record that broke when you added a new sending tool, or a DKIM key that was generated but never actually published. Fix anything that fails here before you touch anything else. The authentication guide covers each record in detail.

Step 2: Check blacklists

If authentication comes back clean, check whether your domain or IP landed on a blacklist. A listing can tank your placement overnight, and it frequently happens with no obvious trigger on your end at all — especially on shared infrastructure.

Run your domain and sending IP through a blacklist checker. If something turns up listed, find that specific blacklist's delisting process, fix whatever caused the listing first, then submit the request. Delisting without addressing the root cause just gets you relisted shortly after.

Step 3: Audit your list quality

A high bounce rate reads as a spammer signal, and it snowballs quickly. If your last campaign bounced above 3 percent, the list itself is the problem, and it's actively hurting your reputation with every additional send.

Stop sending to that list immediately. Run it through an email verifier, remove every invalid and risky address, and only resume with what's left clean. Going forward, validate on import so a bad list never even reaches a live campaign — Sendbox handles this automatically. The bounce rate guide covers the full picture, including the secure email gateways that bounce even legitimate addresses.

Step 4: Review your volume and ramp

Sending too much too fast, from a domain that hasn't earned it yet, is a classic self-inflicted problem. If you recently doubled your volume or added new mailboxes and skipped warmup, that's likely your answer.

Pull volume back down to a conservative per-mailbox level and hold it there for a while. New mailboxes need a proper warmup ramp before they carry real campaigns. Spreading volume across more mailboxes at a lighter per-mailbox rate is almost always the safer path over pushing a small number of them hard.

Step 5: Fix obvious content problems

Now, finally, content. Not because it never matters — it just rarely matters until the first four steps are already clean. Run your template through the free spam checker and strip out the obvious triggers: spammy phrasing, heavy links, oversized images, shouty formatting.

Keep cold email short and plain. A three-line plain-text message from a clean setup will consistently beat a polished HTML email sent from a broken one.

Step 6: Rebuilding reputation

If reputation is already damaged, everything above stops the bleeding, but it doesn't heal the wound on its own. Healing comes from controlled, low-volume sending that steadily generates positive engagement over time.

Pull the affected mailboxes out of active campaigns and run warmup on them to rebuild engagement signals from scratch. Only put them back into rotation once health metrics have actually recovered. With Sendbox you can watch per-mailbox reply and bounce rate to know exactly when a mailbox is safe to use again.

How long recovery actually takes

Set your expectations honestly here. Fixing authentication or a bad list is immediate. Blacklist delisting typically takes 24 to 72 hours once the underlying cause is resolved. Reputation rebuilding takes two to four weeks of careful, patient sending. There's no button that instantly resets a burned domain.

The better path is avoiding this situation entirely: solid infrastructure, real authentication, validated lists, and a genuine warmup ramp from the start. If you're rebuilding from the ground up anyway, it's worth fixing the foundation now so you're not back here in another month.

faqs.question: Why did my cold email deliverability suddenly drop?
faqs.answer: The usual suspects, roughly in order of likelihood: an authentication record silently broke, your domain or IP got blacklisted, you sent to an unvalidated list and bounces spiked, or you ramped up volume without a proper warmup. Work through them in that order.

faqs.question: How do I know if my domain is blacklisted?
faqs.answer: Run your sending domain and IP through a blacklist checker that scans the major DNSBL and RBL databases. If you turn up listed, fix whatever caused it first, then follow that specific blacklist's delisting process. Delisting before fixing the cause just leads straight back to relisting.

faqs.question: Can I fix deliverability without pausing my campaigns?
faqs.answer: Authentication and content fixes can happen while campaigns keep running. But if reputation is already damaged or your list turned out bad, you need to pause the affected mailboxes. Continuing to push mail through a damaged mailbox only slows recovery down.

faqs.question: Should I just buy a new domain instead of fixing the old one?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, if the domain is badly burned. But a fresh domain starts at zero reputation and needs a full warmup, and if you don't fix whatever practices burned the first one, you'll almost certainly burn the second too. Fix the underlying process regardless of which path you take.

faqs.question: How long should I warm up a mailbox before sending again?
faqs.answer: For a mailbox in recovery, budget two to three weeks of warmup before putting it back into real campaigns, and only re-enable it once bounce and engagement metrics have actually recovered. A brand-new mailbox follows the same ramp from day one.

faqs.question: Does sending plain text instead of HTML improve deliverability?
faqs.answer: It helps at the margins. Plain, link-light email avoids content-based spam triggers and reads more like a normal human message. But it's a step-five fix — if your authentication or list is broken, switching to plain text alone won't save you.
